metadata.title: Yet another proof of Brooks' theorem

nodes.name: Brooks' Theorem
nodes.statement_clean: Every graph whose chromatic number equals its maximum degree plus one (and is at least 4) contains a clique of size Delta+1.

nodes.name: Proof of Brooks' Theorem (Rabern's variant)
nodes.statement_latex: By contradiction on a minimum counterexample $G$: extract a maximal independent set $M$, find an induced $K_\Delta$ or odd cycle $T$ in $G - M$, and glue two non-adjacent vertices in $N(T)$ to obtain a smaller $K_{\Delta+1}$-free graph that is $\Delta$-colorable; then extend the coloring greedily to $T$.

nodes.name: Set up minimal counterexample and deduce $\Delta$-regularity
nodes.statement_latex: Suppose the theorem fails and pick a counterexample $G$ minimizing $\card{G}$. Set $\Delta \DefinedAs \Delta(G)$. Minimality gives $\chi(G - v) \le \Delta$ for all $v \in V(G)$, so $G$ is $\Delta$-regular.

nodes.name: Extract induced $K_\Delta$ or odd cycle $T$ from $G - M$
nodes.statement_latex: Let $M$ be a maximal independent set in $G$. Since $\Delta(G - M) < \Delta$ and $\chi(G - M) \ge \Delta$, minimality of $\card{G}$ yields an induced subgraph $T \subseteq G - M$ with $T = K_\Delta$, or $T$ an odd cycle when $\Delta = 3$.

nodes.name: Rule out $K_{\Delta+1}$ minus an edge
nodes.statement_latex: If $G$ contained $K_{\Delta+1} - xy = D \subseteq G$, we could $\Delta$-color $G - D$, give $x$ and $y$ the same color, and finish greedily on $D$, contradicting that $G$ is a counterexample. Hence $G$ contains no $K_{\Delta+1}$ less an edge.

nodes.name: Pick non-adjacent $x,y \in N(T)$ and form glued graph $H$
nodes.statement_latex: Since $K_{\Delta+1} \not\subseteq G$, $\card{N(T)} \ge 2$. Take distinct $x, y \in N(T)$ and define $H \DefinedAs G - T$ if $xy \in E(G)$ and $H \DefinedAs (G - T) + xy$ otherwise. Then $H$ contains no $K_{\Delta+1}$ (else $G$ would contain $K_{\Delta+1}$ less an edge).

nodes.name: Color $H$ and extend to $T$
nodes.statement_latex: By minimality of $\card{G}$, $H$ is $\Delta$-colorable, giving a $\Delta$-coloring of $G - T$ in which $x$ and $y$ receive different colors. Each vertex of $T$ has $\Delta - 1$ available colors and some pair of vertices in $T$ have distinct available sets, so the coloring extends greedily to all of $G$ — contradiction.

nodes.name: Chromatic number $\chi(G)$
nodes.statement_latex: $\chi(G)$ denotes the minimum number of colors needed to properly color the vertices of a graph $G$ so that adjacent vertices receive distinct colors.

nodes.name: Maximum degree $\Delta(G)$
nodes.statement_latex: $\Delta(G)$ denotes the maximum vertex degree in a graph $G$.

nodes.name: Maximal independent set
nodes.statement_latex: An independent set $M \subseteq V(G)$ is maximal if no proper superset of $M$ is independent in $G$.

nodes.name: Complete graph $K_n$
nodes.statement_latex: $K_n$ denotes the complete graph (clique) on $n$ vertices.

nodes.name: Motivation: simplest variation
nodes.statement_latex: A referee for \emph{Brooks' Theorem and Beyond} asked the author to make this proof public. The proof is arguably the simplest variation since it avoids reducing to the cubic case entirely.
